key_terms.meaning: A drive that carries power through a belt, chain or rope which bends around pulleys or sprockets, allowing large shaft spacing and slight misalignment.
Both pulleys turn the same way and the belt does not cross itself; angle of lap on the small pulley is less than 180°.
The belt crosses over, so the pulleys turn in opposite directions and the lap angle exceeds 180° on both.
Loss of speed caused by unequal stretching of the belt on the tight and slack sides as it passes over the pulley.
Relative motion between belt and pulley rim when friction is not enough to carry the load; the cause of speed loss in belt drives.
T<sub>c</sub> = m·v², where m = belt mass per metre (kg/m) and v = belt speed (m/s); it reduces the useful friction grip.
T = σ·b·t, where σ = allowable stress (N/mm²), b = belt width (mm), t = belt thickness (mm).
T₁/T₂ = e^(μθ) for a flat belt, where T₁ = tight side tension, T₂ = slack side tension, μ = coefficient of friction, θ = angle of lap in radians.
The arc of pulley rim actually covered by the belt; for an open belt it is smaller on the small pulley, so that pulley sets the power limit.
P = (T₁ − T₂)·v, where T₁ and T₂ are in newtons and v = belt speed in m/s, giving P in watts.
The included angle of the V-groove in the pulley; the belt wedges into it and the normal reaction is split by β about the groove centre line.
μ′ = μ/sin β, where β is the half groove angle; for β = 17–20° this is about three times the plain μ.
z = P<sub>design</sub> / (rated power per belt × correction factors); V-drives are rated as a whole number of standard belts.
The rise and fall of each chain link as it travels as a chord of the sprocket polygon, giving a periodic speed fluctuation of the chain.
The distance between the centres of two adjacent rollers (mm); it fixes the chain size, the sprocket pitch circle and the load per link.
The tensile load at which the chain fails; the working load must be kept below it by a factor of safety that falls as speed rises.
The direction and pattern in which wires are twisted into strands and strands into rope: regular lay, lang lay, and right-hand or left-hand lay.
σ<sub>b</sub> = E<sub>r</sub>·d<sub>w</sub>/D, where E<sub>r</sub> = rope modulus (about 80–90 GPa), d<sub>w</sub> = wire diameter, D = sheave diameter.
Ratio of sheave tread diameter to rope diameter; keeping it large (typically 20 to 40 or more) keeps bending stress and fatigue low.

takeaways: A flexible drive trades the rigid grip of gears for reach and tolerance of misalignment, and what it loses is either slip (belts) or a strict lubrication need (chains, ropes).
The whole design of a flat belt comes from T₁/T₂ = e^(μθ) and P = (T₁ − T₂)v, so belt width is fixed by the strength limit and friction fixes the tension ratio.
A V-belt multiplies friction by 1/sin β, roughly three times, so it can work with short centres and small pulleys; the price is that the drive is sold and rated in whole numbers of belts.
Chain drives give an exact velocity ratio because there is no slip, but chordal action, wear at the joints, and the need for continuous lubrication are built into the design.
Wire rope is a tension-only member; its strength is the sum of many small wires, and its life is decided as much by sheave diameter as by the breaking load.
Selecting any flexible element means comparing a design load (after service, duty and life factors) with a catalogue rating, then checking the strength condition with a factor of safety.
Misalignment, over-tensioning and under-tensioning cause most belt failures in the field; worn sprockets and dry pins cause most chain failures.
In a wire rope, bending stress repeats every time the rope passes over a sheave, so fatigue — not simple tension — often limits the sheave size.
bank_note: Long answers here are expected to pair a derivation (tension ratio, friction in a groove, bending stress in a rope) with a sizing calculation and a short justification of the drive type chosen.

bank.q: Classify the flexible drives used for power transmission. Compare belts, chains and wire ropes on slip, velocity ratio, centre distance, lubrication and typical applications.
outline: Belts: friction drive, some slip and creep, moderate centres, no lubrication in the open, used for fans, pumps, compressors.
Chains: positive drive through rollers and sprocket teeth, exact velocity ratio, short to moderate centres, needs lubrication and accurate alignment.
Wire rope: tension member gripped by friction on a grooved drum or sheave, long spans, used in hoists and lifts.
Comparison table on slip, velocity ratio accuracy, shock absorbing ability, cost and maintenance.
State that all three allow shafts to be far apart and tolerate small misalignment, unlike gears.

bank.q: Discuss belt materials and belt construction. What properties must a belt material have, and how are flat belts joined into an endless loop?
outline: Materials: leather (oak-tanned), rubberised fabric, balata, cotton, synthetic (nylon, polyester, aramid) reinforced rubber.
Required properties: high tensile strength, low extensibility, high coefficient of friction, flexibility, resistance to moisture, oil and heat.
Flat belt construction: layers of fabric plies bonded in rubber, thickness t built up by plying.
Joints: laced, hinged metal, and cemented or vulcanised endless joints.
V-belt construction: tension cords (polyester, rayon, aramid), rubber body, fabric-wrapped or raw-edge, and the wedge cross-section.

bank.q: Derive the relation T₁/T₂ = e^(μθ) for a flat belt drive and state the assumptions made.
outline: Consider a small element of belt subtending dθ, with tensions T and T + dT.
Radial force balance: normal reaction dN = T·dθ (belt mass neglected) or dN = (T − T<sub>c</sub>)dθ when centrifugal tension is included.
Friction limit: dF = μ·dN = T·dθ combined with dT = μ·T·dθ.
Integrate from slack side to tight side: ln(T₁/T₂) = μθ.
Assumptions: belt is massless/inextensible, friction is at the limiting value over the whole lap, pulley rim is smooth, no slip.

bank.q: Explain chordal action in a chain drive. What are its effects and how are they reduced in design?
outline: The chain wraps the sprocket as a polygon, each link acting as a chord.
Speed of the chain varies between v·cos(180°/z) and v, where z = number of teeth.
Angle of the link at entry and exit changes, giving vertical and horizontal vibration.
Effects: fluctuating velocity, extra dynamic load, noise, wear.
Reduction: use more teeth (z ≥ 17 to 19 for the small sprocket), smaller pitch, moderate speed, and even number of links.

bank.q: Describe the construction of a wire rope and explain regular lay, lang lay, and right-hand and left-hand lay, with the use of each.
outline: Wires are twisted into strands, strands are laid around a fibre or steel core.
Core supports the strands and stores lubricant; fibre core gives flexibility, steel core gives strength.
Designation such as 6×19 means 6 strands of 19 wires each.
Regular lay: wires in a strand run opposite to the strands, giving low twist and resistance to crushing.
Lang lay: wires and strands run the same way, giving more flexibility and wear resistance but a tendency to unlay.
Right-hand and left-hand lay chosen so that the rope tightens on the drum as it is wound.

bank.q: A flat belt transmits 15 kW at a belt speed of 15 m/s between two pulleys of 300 mm and 900 mm diameter with a centre distance of 2.5 m. If μ = 0.3 and the maximum permissible stress in the belt is 2.5 N/mm², determine the belt width for a belt 10 mm thick.
outline: Compute the angle of lap on the smaller pulley from the open-belt geometry: θ = π − 2·sin⁻¹((D − d)/2C).
Find the tight and slack side tensions from P = (T₁ − T₂)v and T₁/T₂ = e^(μθ).
Include centrifugal tension T<sub>c</sub> = mv² and use T₁ = σ·b·t − T<sub>c</sub>.
Solve for width b and round up to a standard width.
Mention that the small pulley governs the design and state the condition θ ≥ 2.6 rad typically.

bank.q: A V-belt drive is to transmit 20 kW from a 1440 rpm motor to a compressor at 480 rpm. Groove half angle β = 18°, μ = 0.12, centre distance 800 mm, small pulley pitch diameter 150 mm. Explain how you would select the number of standard V-belts.
outline: Speed ratio i = 1440/480 = 3, so large pulley pitch diameter = 450 mm.
Virtual or equivalent arc of contact and lap angle θ<sub>d</sub> = π − 2 sin⁻¹((D − d)/2C), then correction factor for arc of contact.
Effective friction μ/sin β gives the tension ratio T₁/T₂ = e^((μ/sin β)θ).
Design power = transmitted power × service factor for a compressor duty, then further correction for belt length.
Number of belts z = design power / rated power per belt from the manufacturer's chart, rounded up.

bank.q: Design a roller chain drive to transmit 10 kW at 1000 rpm of the small sprocket to a machine at 400 rpm. State the selection steps and the checks you would carry out.
outline: Speed ratio, choice of number of teeth on the small sprocket (z₁ not less than about 17), then z₂ = z₁ × i.
Estimate pitch from the power–speed–pitch rating chart or the empirical relation, and pick a standard pitch.
Compute pitch circle diameters, chain length in pitches, corrected centre distance.
Check the chain tension against the breaking load with a factor of safety that depends on speed and duty.
Check bearing pressure on the roller pins and state the lubrication method (manual, drip, bath, spray).

bank.q: A wire rope hoist lifts a load of 20 kN. The rope runs over a sheave with a diameter-to-rope-diameter ratio of 25. Select the rope construction and diameter, given a permissible wire stress and a factor of safety of 6.
outline: Choose construction, e.g. 6×19 for a general hoist with a fibre core, and state why.
Total tensile load = load plus the rope's own weight plus the bending and acceleration effects.
Equivalent load = direct tension + bending load; bending stress from σ<sub>b</sub> = E<sub>r</sub>·d<sub>w</sub>/D, with d<sub>w</sub> from the rope diameter and construction.
Multiply the working load by the factor of safety to get the required breaking strength and read the rope diameter from the manufacturer's table.
Check the sheave diameter ratio and state that a larger D/d improves fatigue life.

bank.q: Explain step by step how the length of an open belt between two pulleys of diameter d and D with centre distance C is found, and how the same geometry gives the angle of lap.
outline: Length L = (π/2)(D + d) + 2C + (D − d)²/(4C) for an open belt.
Angle of lap on the smaller pulley θ<sub>s</sub> = π − 2α and on the larger θ<sub>l</sub> = π + 2α, where sin α = (D − d)/2C.
State that for a crossed belt the lap angle is π + 2α on both pulleys.
Use the smaller lap in the tension-ratio equation because it limits power.
Note the practical limits: centre distance should be between about 1.5(D + d) and 3(D + d), and the lap on the small pulley must not fall below about 2.6 rad.

bank.q: For a given duty, compare flat belt, V-belt and chain drives and justify which one you would choose where the centre distance is short, the speed ratio is high and no slip can be tolerated.
outline: Flat belt: needs long centres and large pulleys for adequate lap, allows slip, poor for high ratios.
V-belt: wedging action multiplies friction, works on short centres with small pulleys, still a friction drive so slip is possible under overload.
Chain: positive drive, no slip, exact ratio, but needs lubrication and alignment and adds polygonal speed variation.
Recommend the chain for zero-slip requirement, with the V-belt as the cheaper alternative if slight slip is acceptable.
Support the answer with the tension-ratio and effective-friction relations.

bank.q: Explain why replacing a flat pulley by a V-grooved pulley greatly increases the power that can be carried for the same belt tension, and discuss the side effects of that increase on the shaft and bearing design.
outline: In a groove the normal reaction on each flank is N, and its vertical components add up so effective friction becomes μ/sin β.
With β = 18°, 1/sin β ≈ 3.2, so the usable tension ratio e^(μθ/sin β) is much larger for the same μ and θ.
A larger T₁/T₂ ratio means more power for the same maximum tension, or the same power with a smaller belt and smaller pulleys.
Side effects: higher wedging means larger radial load on the shaft and bearings, and the groove angle must be maintained or the belt sinks and slips.
Conclusion: the gain in power density is paid for in bearing load and in tighter alignment and groove-angle tolerances.

bank.q: A wire rope fails repeatedly in service at the same place near a sheave. Analyse the likely causes and explain how each of tension, bending, sheave size and lay affects rope life.
outline: Fatigue from repeated bending as each wire passes over the sheave; bending stress varies as E<sub>r</sub>·d<sub>w</sub>/D, so a small sheave is the main culprit.
Tension alone is checked by the factor of safety; combined tension plus bending is the real working condition.
Sheave and drum diameter ratio D/d, groove radius, and fleet angle of the rope on the drum.
Lay: lang lay is more flexible and wears better on the outside but is prone to unlaying; regular lay resists crushing.
Also consider corrosion, incorrect lubrication, shock loading, rope being reversed over small sheaves, and end termination details.

bank.q: Discuss the modes of failure of a roller chain drive and explain how lubrication and sprocket tooth count influence each mode.
outline: Failure modes: fatigue of the link plates, wear of pins and bushings (elongation), roller and bushing impact, and tooth wear on the sprocket.
Elongation from pin wear changes the pitch line and causes the chain to ride high on the teeth, leading to jumping.
Fewer teeth increase chordal action and the load per tooth, so the small sprocket should have at least 17 to 19 teeth.
Lubrication: manual, drip, bath or slinger, and spray, chosen with chain speed and power.
High speed demands continuous oil supply; dry running causes rapid pin and bushing wear and noise.

bank.q: A plant must choose between a chain drive and a V-belt drive for a crusher that experiences heavy starting torque and shock. Evaluate both options and recommend one with reasons.
outline: Crusher duty implies shock and overload, so the drive's ability to absorb shock matters.
A V-belt has some elasticity and slips under overload, acting as a mechanical fuse; it also damps shocks.
A chain is positive and transmits shock directly to the shafts and bearings, though it keeps exact ratio and needs less centre distance.
Compare efficiency, maintenance, lubrication, cost and overload protection.
A common practical answer: V-belt drive with a service factor well above 1, plus check of belt number and pulley size; state the trade-off clearly.

glossary.def: An endless flexible band that transmits power between two pulleys by friction.
A belt of rectangular cross-section that runs on a flat or slightly crowned pulley rim.
A belt of trapezoidal cross-section that wedges into a grooved pulley to gain extra friction.
A series of linked rollers or pins that transmits power by engaging the teeth of two sprockets.
A toothed wheel whose teeth engage the chain rollers and so drive it without slip.
A grooved wheel over which a rope runs, used in hoists and rope drives.
A tension member made by twisting steel wires into strands and strands into a rope around a core.
A group of wires twisted together in a helix, several of which are laid up to form a wire rope.
The central member of a wire rope, of fibre or steel, that supports the strands and holds lubricant.
The helical pattern and direction in which wires and strands are twisted to form a rope.
The centre-to-centre distance between two adjacent chain rollers, measured along the chain.
The diameter of the circle on which the chain rollers or belt centre line sit when wrapped on the sprocket or pulley.
The arc of the pulley or sheave actually covered by the belt or rope, expressed in radians.
The ratio of the limiting friction force to the normal reaction between belt and pulley.
The small relative motion between belt and pulley caused by unequal elastic stretch on the two sides.
Gross relative sliding between belt and pulley that occurs when the required friction exceeds the available friction.
The tension induced in a moving belt or rope by its own mass as it travels round the pulley.
A small extra pulley used to increase the angle of lap or to take up slack in a belt drive.
The periodic variation in chain speed caused by the chain wrapping a sprocket as a polygon rather than a circle.
The ratio of the failure load or stress to the working load or stress, applied to cover uncertainty and duty.
The tensile load at which a chain, rope or belt actually fractures in a pull test.
The included angle of a V-belt pulley groove, usually 34° to 40°, which sets the wedging gain.
A multiplier applied to the transmitted power to account for the nature of the driven machine and its hours of duty.
The joint by which a flat belt is made endless, by lacing, metal fasteners, or cementing and vulcanising.
